KYC software: what banks need it to do

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 20, 2026•9 min read

KYC software is the set of tools a bank uses to collect a customer's identifying information, verify it, screen the customer against government lists, record what it found and keep the file current. US rules do not name a product. They set what a bank's written procedures must do, mainly in the customer identification program (CIP) rule at 31 CFR 1020.220, the beneficial ownership rule at 31 CFR 1010.230 and the ongoing due diligence element of the AML program rule at 31 CFR 1020.210. The software is how a team runs those procedures and shows an examiner that it ran them.

This guide covers what KYC tools do, what a system has to support, recent changes, how to evaluate a vendor and how a team runs it. It uses the bank rules; the beneficial ownership rule points to parallel CIP rules for broker-dealers, mutual funds and futures firms. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What KYC software does

Most KYC solutions combine several of these functions:

  • Data collection: application forms and APIs that capture each customer's name, date of birth, address and identification number, and the owners and controllers of a business.
  • Identity verification: checking an identity document, or comparing what the customer gave with information from a consumer reporting agency, public database or other source.
  • Screening: comparing the customer with sanctions and other government lists.
  • Risk rating: scoring the customer from what the bank knows about them and the account.
  • Case management: a queue where discrepancies and hits go to a reviewer, with the decision recorded.
  • Records and refresh: storing what was collected and checked, and running periodic or event-driven reviews.

Vendors that use the label KYC AML software often mean the platform also feeds or runs ongoing monitoring. The AML program rule keeps customer due diligence going after the account is open, so the monitoring side belongs in the evaluation too.

What the rules ask the software to support

The CIP rule requires a written program "appropriate for the bank's size and type of business", with risk-based procedures that "enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer."

RequirementRuleWhat to check in the software
Obtain name, date of birth (for individuals), address and an identification number before opening an account1020.220(a)(2)(i)Required fields for each customer type, including the non-US person options such as passport number and country of issuance
Verify identity within a reasonable time after opening, by documents, non-documentary methods or both1020.220(a)(2)(ii)Both methods, with fallbacks for a customer who cannot present a photo ID or opens the account without appearing in person
Respond when identity cannot be verified1020.220(a)(2)(iii)Account states for not opening, limited use while verification continues and closure, plus a route to suspicious activity report (SAR) review
Keep records of identifying information, documents relied on, verification methods and results, and "the resolution of any substantive discrepancy"1020.220(a)(3)A record of each step and reviewer decision, kept five years after the account closes for identifying information and five years after the record is made for the rest
Check customers against any list of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organizations that Treasury designates for this purpose1020.220(a)(4)A way to add a designated list and check it within a reasonable period after opening, or earlier if another federal law, regulation or directive requires
Give customers notice before they open an account1020.220(a)(5)Notice text built into each channel's application flow
Identify each individual who owns 25 percent or more of a legal entity customer, and one individual with significant responsibility to control it1010.230(b) and (d)Fields for up to four owners and one control person, the certification, and verification of each owner
Ongoing due diligence: a customer risk profile, and monitoring that on a risk basis keeps customer information, including beneficial owners, up to date1020.210(a)(2)(v)A risk profile per customer, review triggers and periodic review dates

The CIP rule also lets a bank rely on another financial institution for parts of its CIP. The reliance has to be reasonable, the other institution has to be subject to an AML program rule and regulated by a Federal functional regulator, and it has to sign a contract to certify every year that it has implemented its AML program and will perform the specified CIP requirements. A software vendor running checks for the bank is a third-party relationship instead, covered by the guidance below.

On the list check, the FFIEC BSA/AML manual notes that, as of its publication date, "no designated government lists for CIP purposes exist", and that checks against OFAC lists and section 314(a) requests "remain separate and distinct requirements." Our guide to reviewing a sanctions screening hit covers the OFAC side.

What changed in 2025 and 2026

TIN from a third-party source

On June 27, 2025, the OCC, FDIC and NCUA, with FinCEN's concurrence, issued an order that lets banks under their jurisdiction obtain a customer's taxpayer identification number (TIN) from a third-party source instead of from the customer. The Federal Reserve issued its own order for banks under its jurisdiction on July 31, 2025. A bank using either order must otherwise comply with the CIP rule, including procedures to obtain TIN information before opening the account, and both orders say use of the exemption is optional. The CIP rule already allowed third-party collection for credit card accounts. For software, the question is which source supplies the TIN and whether the record shows it.

Owner checks at each new account

FinCEN's order FIN-2026-R001, issued February 13, 2026, lets covered financial institutions stop identifying and verifying a legal entity customer's beneficial owners every time the customer opens an account. They may limit that work to the first account, to times when they know of facts that "would reasonably call into question the reliability" of the information they hold, and to what their risk-based ongoing due diligence calls for. In that last case, the institution may rely on information it already holds if the customer certifies or confirms, verbally or in writing, that it is up to date and accurate, and it must keep a record of that confirmation. Using the relief is at the institution's discretion. A system that forces a fresh ownership form on every new account, or cannot record a verbal confirmation, makes the relief hard to use.

A proposed change to the due diligence rule

On November 17, 2026, FinCEN issued a proposed rule to strengthen customer due diligence requirements, as part of Treasury's implementation of Executive Order 14406. It is a proposal, so the current rule text still applies. Ask vendors how quickly they can change required fields and review rules once a final rule is published.

How to evaluate KYC software

Buying KYC compliance software, or a wider AML KYC software suite, creates a third-party relationship. The Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management, issued by the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC in June 2023, says banks must operate safely and soundly and comply with applicable laws whether they do the work themselves or through a third party, and that using a third party "does not diminish its responsibility to meet these requirements to the same extent as if its activities were performed by the banking organization in-house." The guidance follows a relationship through planning, due diligence and third-party selection, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring and termination. Our vendor due diligence use case shows how that review runs.

For a KYC system, those stages become practical questions:

  • Can every requirement in the table above be configured to match your written procedure, by customer type, product and channel?
  • Does each case keep the data, its source, the method, the result and the reviewer's decision, in a form an examiner or independent tester can follow?
  • Will you have appropriate access to data and information from the vendor? The guidance lists that check among management's responsibilities.
  • How does the vendor handle list updates, data source changes and its own releases, and how will you hear about them?
  • Do its disaster recovery and business continuity plans specify the time frame to resume activities and recover data, as the guidance describes?
  • If the system scores risk or matches names with a model, how will you validate it? Our note on SR 26-2 covers the model risk guidance that replaced SR 11-7.

Run a pilot before switching. The December 2018 Joint Statement on Innovative Efforts to Combat Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, from the Federal Reserve, FDIC, FinCEN, NCUA and OCC, says "pilot programs in and of themselves should not subject banks to supervisory criticism even if the pilot programs ultimately prove unsuccessful." It also says banks must continue to meet their BSA/AML obligations while they develop pilots.

How a bank operations team runs KYC software

  1. Start from the written procedure. Write the CIP and due diligence steps first: what to collect per customer type, which verification method applies when, and what counts as a substantive discrepancy. Then configure the software to match.
  2. Set collection by channel. Build the required fields and the customer notice into each application flow, online and in branch, and decide whether the TIN comes from the customer or a third-party source.
  3. Set verification and fallbacks. Choose documentary checks, non-documentary checks or both, and define what happens when one fails, for example when a customer opens online and cannot present a photo ID.
  4. Decide what goes to a person. Screening hits, data mismatches, missing owners and high risk ratings should reach a named reviewer queue with the evidence attached.
  5. Work the queue and record each decision. The reviewer resolves the case, and the record shows how any substantive discrepancy was resolved.
  6. Follow the cannot-verify path. When identity cannot be verified, apply the procedure: do not open, limit use while verification continues, close, or refer the case for SAR review.
  7. Keep files current. Re-screen when lists change, run periodic reviews on the schedule your risk ratings set, and refresh beneficial ownership when facts call it into question.
  8. Test after every change. Include the software in independent testing, and test again after vendor releases, rule changes and data source changes.

For these steps in practice, see KYC onboarding review, periodic KYC review and, for business customers, KYB and beneficial ownership. Common questions

Do regulators require a particular KYC software?

No. The CIP rule sets what the written procedures must do, scaled to the bank's size and type of business, and names no product or vendor.

Is the bank responsible if a vendor's checks are wrong?

The bank stays responsible for compliance. The 2023 guidance from the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC says using a third party does not diminish a bank's responsibility to comply, to the same extent as if it did the work in-house.

Do we collect owner information again for each new account?

For a legal entity customer, not if you use FinCEN's February 2026 order. You can limit it to the first account, facts that question the information you hold, and what your ongoing due diligence calls for, with a recorded customer confirmation when you rely on earlier information.
